summary: Defines an Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) extension for provisioning and managing DNSSEC data for domain names held in a shared registry. It is written in XML and extends the EPP domain name mapping. It is a Proposed Standard and replaced RFC 4310.

plainLanguage.summary: When you register a website name, you may also want to sign it for safety. This adds a way for registrars to hand the signing details to the registry.

subtitle: How a registrar tells a domain registry about a domain's DNSSEC keys, using an extension to the EPP domain mapping.

tldr.problem: A parent zone needs to know which keys sign a child zone before it can vouch for them. Domain registries needed a standard way for their clients to hand over that DNSSEC data.
tldr.mechanism: The mapping adds secDNS elements, in XML, to the EPP domain commands. A client sends either Delegation Signer (DS) data or raw key data, and the server publishes or generates DS records from it.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5910 defines secDNS-1.1, which deprecates secDNS-1.0 from RFC 4310, with safer removal of records, add and remove in one update, and support for servers that accept only key data.

today: RFC 5910 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 4310. The metadata for this RFC lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the Extension Does
sections.content:
This document is an extension of the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) version 1.0 (RFC 5730) and of the EPP domain name mapping (RFC 5731). It is specified in XML and XML Schema. Readers are expected to know EPP, the DNS and the DNS security extensions of RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035.

The mapping provides a way to provision and manage DNSSEC data for domain names held in a shared central repository. Information exchanged this way can be extracted from the repository and used to publish Delegation Signer (DS) resource records, as described in RFC 4034.

It obsoletes RFC 4310, so secDNS-1.1 deprecates secDNS-1.0. The reasons given are:

  • Removing DS data by the non-unique keyTag element was ambiguous. The client must now name all four DS fields, which are guaranteed to be unique.
  • A single command can now both add and remove DS data, as in RFC 5731.
  • The chg element is used consistently with RFC 5731, to change attribute values rather than replace DS data.
  • A new Key Data Interface supports "thick" DNSSEC servers that accept only key data and generate the DS data.
sections.plainLanguage: A registry keeps the big list of website names. This tells registrars exactly how to give it the secret-handshake details that prove a name is genuine.

sections.title: Migrating from RFC 4310
sections.content:
If a server announces support for both versions in the EPP greeting, clients that support both SHOULD prefer secDNS-1.1. A server moving from the old version SHOULD support both for a reasonable migration period.

Which version the server returns in a domain info response SHOULD depend on the extURI elements the client listed in its login command. If secDNS-1.1 was listed, the server returns version 1.1, even if 1.0 was listed too. If only secDNS-1.0 was listed, it returns version 1.0. If neither was listed, it does not return the infData element at all.
sections.plainLanguage: When a shop changes its order form, it keeps accepting the old form for a while. Customers who ask for the new form get the new answers.

sections.title: DS Data Interface and Key Data Interface
sections.content:
A server supports one of two interfaces. In the DS Data Interface, the client creates the DS information and passes it for adds and removes, and the server returns DS information in domain info responses. In the Key Data Interface, the client passes only key data and the server generates the DS information according to its policy.

A dsData element holds a keyTag (an unsignedShort), an alg, a digestType and a digest (hexBinary). It may also hold an optional keyData element that the server can use for validation. A keyData element holds flags, protocol, alg and pubKey, where pubKey is base64Binary with a minimum length of 1. These map to the DS and DNSKEY record fields of RFC 4034. The key data SHOULD have the Secure Entry Point (SEP) bit set.

Within one command or response the two forms MUST NOT be mixed, apart from keyData inside dsData for validation. A server must use only one form across all create, update and info elements, except during a transition period. A client can switch by removing everything with rem and all set to true, then adding data in the new form. A command using an unsupported interface gets error result code 2306.
sections.plainLanguage: You can hand over either the finished fingerprint card, or the raw ingredients and let the registry make the card. A server picks one way and sticks to it.

sections.title: Maximum Signature Lifetime
sections.content:
The optional maxSigLife element is a child's preference for the number of seconds after signature generation when the parent's signature on the DS information will expire. It applies to the RRSIG record over the DS RRset. The value is in seconds, in an extended XML Schema int format restricted to a minimum of 1.

If the client gives no value, or the server does not support the one requested, the server operator's default signature expiration policy applies. That policy is learned out of band.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like asking how long a stamp of approval should stay valid. If the registry does not like your number, it uses its own rule.

sections.title: How the EPP Commands Change
sections.content:
The extension adds nothing to the check, delete, renew or transfer commands. It adds elements to info responses, and to the create and update commands.

In an info response, the extension element SHOULD contain a secDNS:infData element if the domain has such data and server policy allows. It carries an optional maxSigLife and one or more dsData or keyData elements, but not both. A create command contains a secDNS:create element with an optional maxSigLife and zero or more dsData or keyData elements. If maxSigLife is unsupported, error 2102 MUST be returned.

An update command contains a secDNS:update element with at least one of add, rem or chg. The server MUST remove first and then add, so the order of rem and add matters. In rem, the all element removes all DS and key data when true. Removing a key could remove more than one DS record, since there can be more than one per key. Removing all DS information can remove the parent's ability to secure the delegation.

The update element also takes an optional urgent attribute, default false, asking for high priority. A server that does not support it returns 2102, and one that supports it but cannot complete the update with high priority returns 2306.
sections.plainLanguage: The same forms you already use to register a name get a few extra boxes for the security details. You can add, take away, or change them, and take-aways happen first.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The extension adds no security services beyond those of EPP, the domain mapping and the layers beneath. Transform operations MUST be limited to the sponsoring client, and any other client's attempt MUST be rejected with an authorization error. A trust relationship MUST exist between client and server, and provisioning of public key information MUST only happen after both parties are identified with strong authentication.

Accepting a false key can have significant operational consequences. Parent and child zones MUST be consistent, or the delegation will not appear in the secure namespace and query responses cannot be trusted. If a key is compromised, the client can remove it or update the delegation using the urgent attribute. To remove a secure delegation quickly, first do an urgent update to remove the credentials, then set the domain status to clientHold or serverHold. Deleting the domain is more drastic.

Validity checks and DS creation need computing resources, so a client could cause denial of service, on purpose or by accident. Server operators SHOULD manage command load and SHOULD consider limiting the range of acceptable signature lifetime values.
sections.plainLanguage: Only the person who registered the name may change its security details, and the registry should be sure who is asking. Handing over a wrong key can break the name.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The document registers two URNs under the registry mechanism of RFC 3688, with the IESG as registrant contact. They are the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:secDNS-1.1 and the schema urn:ietf:params:xml:schema:secDNS-1.1. The schema itself is given in the Formal Syntax section of the document.

On internationalization, the extension follows the domain mapping and does not override it. XML supports Unicode, and UTF-8 is RECOMMENDED where parser encoding support is inconsistent.
sections.plainLanguage: The new names for these forms were written into an official list so nobody else uses them.
